newsitem.title: USA: Stocks seen climbing further, narrow focus a risk.
newsitem.headline: Stocks seen climbing further, narrow focus a risk.

text.p: NEW YORK - The stock market is likely to keep shattering records through the end of the year, but some traders are wishing for a Christmas bonus -- that smaller, neglected issues will hop on the bandwagon and reduce chances of a bust.
"A broadening of the advance will be a healthy thing," said a Wall Street trader who declined to be identified.

He said some of the big name stocks that have been the best performers in the rally are at such lofty heights that individual issues could take a severe pounding in the event of some unforeseen disappointment.

"What we have had has been a narrowing of leadership in the market," said Marion Schultheis, vice president and senior portfolio manager at IDS Equity Advisors. She compared it to 1970-72, when most of the action and talk on Wall Street focused on a select group popularly known as the "nifty fifty."

Today's favourites, she said, are companies that analysts believe can deliver dependable earnings growth even if the economy slowed down. In fact most of the companies have a global reach so that overseas business can compensate for any slack in the U.S. economy.

Schultheis and other analysts said while there are some differences of opinion about which stocks are in the new, bigger "nifty fifty," typical candidates are General Electric Co., International Business Machines Corp., Intel Corp., Microsoft Corp. and Compaq Computer Corp.
Other candidates come from the health care area.
"I think between now and the end of the year, money will still flow into those names," Schultheis said.
Trude Latimer, an independent analyst based in Charlottesville, Va., agreed that the smaller issues have taken a back seat.

"For months now, it's been a small handful of stocks that have been doing the whole thing," Latimer said. "When low-priced stocks are moving they're moving for two days. We have not had a real move in stocks selling below $10 unless it's a specific stock and a particularly hot area."

Latimer and others say many individual investors who ordinarily might consider buying a low-priced, small capitalisation stock now do their investing by buying a hot mutual fund. But fund managers might consider these lower-priced stocks too illiquid to buy.
According to Schultheis, one scenario that could unfold in January is a move into cyclical, or economically sensitive, stocks such as those of paper and aluminum companies.
She said this could be a "false rally" and fund managers will have a tough time deciding whether to cut exposure in the current "nifty fifty" group and jump into the cyclicals, or just stand pat.

As for the longer-term outlook, Schultheis thinks "fundamentals for the market are pretty positive for 12 to 18 months. "High valuations by themselves don't mean that stocks will go down." If there is a risk in the market, she said, it is that "the economy is stronger than people are anticipating, rather than weaker."
Schultheis and others agreed that the high valuations for the current "nifty fifty" group cannot be compared with the sky-high valuations given to the favoured few in the early 1970s.

The trader who preferred to be anonymous noted with some irony that the 1970's "nifty fifty" group included some well-known names that went on to disappoint investors later on, including Avon Products Inc., Xerox Corp. and Polaroid Corp. "It took Avon 10 years to recuperate after the bubble burst," he said.
On Friday, the Dow Jones industrial average rallied 22.36 points to close at 6,521.70, up 49.94 on the week. The Nasdaq index rose 5.29 to a record 1,292.61, gaining 18.25 for the week.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 2.02 to 757.02. The index was up 8.29 for the week. The American Stock Exchange index rose 2.84 to 591.48, and added 0.71 on the week.
